title: Privacy is a design choice.
summary: Someone has trusted us with their information. What happens next?

blocks.text: If someone sends us their information, they’re trusting us to look after it. We don’t stop being responsible for it because the form works and the feature has shipped.
That’s where privacy starts for me. Why are we asking for this? What are we going to do with it? Who’s going to look after it? I’d like us to have those answers before we start collecting anything.
Where does it go?
Take a contact form. Someone types a message and presses send. They probably expect it to reach an inbox. They may not expect copies in notifications, logs or backups.
And the message could contain something sensitive we never asked for. People don’t always write neatly within the boundaries we imagined when we designed the form.
Every copy is another place where that information needs looking after. Who can read it? How long does it stay? What happens when it’s no longer needed? Those are part of building the feature too.
Could we explain the choice?
Sometimes we need information to do something useful. Sometimes we ask for it because that’s what the form has always asked for. It’s worth knowing which situation we’re in.
I want to understand what the person gets from sharing it, whether we could do the same thing without it, and how we’ll explain what happens next.
We can change a design before it goes live. Once someone’s information is in our systems, we already have a responsibility to them.

title: Before the diagram, ask a better question.
summary: We’re looking at the same picture. Are we actually agreeing on the same thing?

blocks.text: Two people can look at a diagram, nod along and leave with completely different ideas about how the system works.
One reads an arrow as “send this and wait for an answer”. The other reads it as “send this and get on with the next thing”. Both think they’ve agreed. They haven’t.

Before we get too attached to the boxes, I want to know what we’re trying to decide. Where does a responsibility belong? What happens when something is unavailable? What should the person using it expect?
Let people explain what they see
A quiet room doesn’t tell us much. Give people a chance to explain how they think it works, especially the bits they’re unsure about.

If the explanations don’t match, that’s useful. We’ve found something to work through while it’s still a drawing. I’d rather have that conversation now than discover the difference after we’ve built it.
Try one awkward situation
Here’s an invented example. An application saves an order and sends a message to a warehouse. Now the warehouse is unavailable.
Do we ask the customer to wait? Accept the order and deal with it later? Who knows there’s still work to do?
We need to agree on that behaviour before choosing how the connection works. Drawing a more detailed arrow won’t settle a disagreement about what we’re promising the customer.
Keep the unanswered questions
We don’t have to settle everything in one discussion. If something is an assumption, mark it as one. If we don’t know yet, leave the question where the next person can see it.
By the end, I want us to know what we’ve decided, why we’ve decided it and what’s still open. Then we have something we can build from, question and change when we learn more.
